text: Applicant Tracking Systems parse resumes as plain text and often fail on multi-column layouts, text inside tables, or text embedded in images. Single-column layouts with standard section headings (Experience, Education, Skills) parse most reliably.
Contact information, dates, and job titles should be in plain text, not inside headers, footers, or text boxes, since many ATS parsers skip those regions entirely.
A text-based PDF (exported from Word, Google Docs, or LaTeX) is the safest format for ATS compatibility. Scanned image PDFs cannot be parsed without OCR and should be avoided.

Strong resume bullet points follow an action-verb + task + quantified result structure, for example 'Reduced API response time by 40% by introducing Redis caching' rather than 'Responsible for improving performance'.

Recruiters and ATS keyword scoring both respond better to measurable outcomes: percentages, time saved, revenue, user counts, or scale (e.g. requests/sec, team size) make impact concrete instead of vague.

Resumes that mirror the exact terminology used in the job description (e.g. 'React.js' vs 'ReactJS', 'CI/CD' vs 'continuous integration') score higher on keyword-matching ATS systems, since these systems often do literal string matching.
Resume bullets should be written in the past tense for previous roles and present tense only for current responsibilities, with consistent verb tense throughout each section.
Avoid first-person pronouns (I, my) on a resume; bullets should start directly with an action verb ('Built', 'Led', 'Designed') for a concise, professional tone.

A scannable resume uses consistent formatting: the same date format throughout, consistent heading styles, and reverse-chronological ordering within each section so the most recent and relevant experience appears first.

For early-career or student resumes, a Projects section placed near the top (before or alongside Experience) is effective when formal work experience is limited, since it demonstrates applied skills directly.
A skills section should separate categories (e.g. Languages, Frameworks, Tools, Cloud) rather than listing everything in one unsorted line, which both improves scannability and keyword matching.
Listing a skill only in the Skills section without any supporting evidence in Experience or Projects is a common weakness; skills claimed should be demonstrated at least once in a bullet point.

For software engineering roles, job descriptions commonly weight core skills higher when they appear in the first few required-qualifications bullets, and 'nice to have' sections indicate lower-priority skills.

For full-stack or backend roles, evidence of system design thinking (scalability, data modeling, API design) in project or experience bullets is typically more valued than simply listing a long tool list.

For data analyst or data scientist roles, ATS and recruiters look for specific tooling (SQL, Python, pandas, visualization tools) paired with a described business outcome, not just tool names in isolation.

When a required skill from a job description is missing from a resume, the most effective mitigation (if true) is to relate it to an adjacent skill already present, rather than fabricating direct experience with it.
